items.title: Mutable default arguments
items.question: def add(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items. Calling add(1) then add(2) returns [1, 2]. Why, and what is the fix?
items.answer: Default values are evaluated once, when the def statement executes, and the same list object is reused on every call. Use a sentinel: items=None, then if items is None: items = []. The same applies to dicts, sets, and any other mutable default.

items.title: The global interpreter lock
items.body: CPython's default build has a global interpreter lock: only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help for I/O-bound work because blocking I/O releases the GIL, but CPU-bound pure-Python code does not get faster with more threads.
items.question: What are your options for CPU-bound parallelism?
items.answer: Use multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor, push hot loops into C extensions or NumPy (which release the GIL), or run on the free-threaded CPython build from PEP 703, which removes the GIL at some single-thread cost and requires compatible extensions.

items.title: Blocking calls freeze asyncio
items.question: Why does a single time.sleep(2) or synchronous HTTP call inside an async def handler stall every other request in an asyncio server?
items.answer: asyncio runs all coroutines on one thread and only switches at await points. A blocking call never yields, so the event loop is frozen until it returns. Use async equivalents (asyncio.sleep, an async HTTP client) or offload blocking work with asyncio.to_thread or loop.run_in_executor.

items.title: is vs ==
items.body: == compares values via __eq__; is compares object identity. Use is only for singletons such as None. Small-int and string caching can make is appear to work for equal values, but that is an implementation detail.

items.title: Late-binding closures
items.question: fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]; [f() for f in fns] returns [2, 2, 2]. Why, and how do you get [0, 1, 2]?
items.answer: Closures look up i when they are called, not when they are defined, and all three lambdas share the same i, which ends at 2. Bind the current value as a default argument, lambda i=i: i, or use functools.partial.

source.name: Python Programming FAQ - lambdas in a loop

items.title: Refcounting plus cycle GC
items.body: CPython frees most objects immediately via reference counting. A separate cyclic garbage collector (the gc module) finds reference cycles, such as objects that point to each other, which reference counting alone can never free.

items.title: Generators save memory
items.question: Why can sum(x * x for x in range(10**8)) run in constant memory while sum([x * x for x in range(10**8)]) may exhaust RAM?
items.answer: The generator expression yields values lazily, one at a time, as sum pulls them. The list comprehension materializes all 100 million results first. Generators can only be consumed once, so materialize a list when you need several passes or len().

items.title: Deleting while iterating a dict
items.question: A loop does for k in d: if cond(k): del d[k] and raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. What are clean fixes?
items.answer: Iterate over a snapshot of the keys, for k in list(d): ..., or build a new dict with a comprehension: d = {k: v for k, v in d.items() if not cond(k)}. Changing a dict size during iteration is disallowed because the iterator position would become invalid.
